name: Draksharama (Bhimeswara Temple)
deity: Bhimeswara Swamy, a form of Shiva worshipped as a tall pale lingam; his consort Manikyamba is venerated here as one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas.
summary: Draksharama, in the Godavari delta of Andhra Pradesh, is one of the five Pancharama Kshetras sacred to Shiva. Here Shiva is worshipped as Bhimeswara Swamy in the form of a tall pale lingam rising through two storeys of the shrine, while his consort Manikyamba is honoured as one of the eighteen Maha Shakti Peethas. Long revered as the 'Dakshina Kasi', the town draws pilgrims of both the Shaiva and Shakta traditions.

sections.history: The temple is generally attributed to the Eastern Chalukyas, with tradition connecting its construction to Chalukya Bhima I around the ninth and tenth centuries. Over succeeding generations it was patronised and enlarged by later rulers, and its walls carry a remarkable body of inscriptions from the Eastern Chalukya, Chalukya-Chola and Kakatiya periods. These epigraphs record endowments, land grants and repairs, and make the site one of the most important sources for the medieval history of the Godavari region. Successive dynasties treated Draksharama as a place of prestige, and the temple gradually gained the enclosures, gateways and subsidiary shrines that give it its present scale.
sections.architecture: The temple stands within two concentric prakara, or enclosure walls, entered through gateways aligned to the cardinal directions. The central sanctum is unusual in being built on two levels: the tall lingam of Bhimeswara passes through both storeys, and the upper portion is worshipped from a raised gallery reached by internal stairs. Pillared halls of dark stone surround the shrine, their surfaces carved with figural and decorative work. The separate shrine of Manikyamba lies within the complex, giving the plan its dual Shaiva and Shakta focus. Weathered sculpture, inscribed slabs and a large stepped tank complete an ensemble that reflects Eastern Chalukyan building traditions carried forward under later patrons.
sections.legends: Draksharama is woven into several strands of tradition. Its name is linked to the sage Daksha, whose great sacrifice is placed here in some accounts, so that the town is remembered as Daksha's abode. It is also associated with the sage Vyasa. The temple's central story is the Pancharama legend: when the mighty lingam worshipped by the demon Taraka was broken into five pieces, each fell at a different site and became a self-manifest shrine, Draksharama being one of the five. Tradition further holds that Surya, the Sun god, installed and worshipped the lingam here. The presence of Manikyamba as a Shakti Peetha adds the wider tale of Sati, whose falling form is said to have sanctified the earth.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the foremost festival, when night-long worship and large crowds fill the complex. Because the temple also enshrines Manikyamba as a Shakti Peetha, the autumn Dasara or Navaratri season is celebrated with special devotion to the goddess. Kalyanotsavam, the ceremonial marriage of Bhimeswara and Manikyamba, is another highlight, along with regular monthly and seasonal observances tied to the lunar calendar. During these occasions the town fills with pilgrims, ritual processions and cultural performances.
sections.experience: A visit to Draksharama moves between two devotions. Pilgrims first take darshan of the tall Bhimeswara lingam, climbing to the upper gallery to worship its higher portion, then turn to the shrine of Manikyamba Devi. The complex rewards unhurried walking: shaded pillared halls, weathered carvings and slabs dense with old inscriptions line the enclosures, and a large temple tank offers a quiet pause. Mornings and evenings, when lamps are lit and bells sound, carry the strongest atmosphere. The surrounding delta town is small and devotional in character, and many visitors combine Draksharama with the other Pancharama shrines as part of a longer pilgrimage.

visit.timings: The temple generally opens early in the morning and again in the evening, with a midday break, following the usual pattern for major Andhra temples. Exact darshan and archana timings change on festival days, so verify the current schedule locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest, traditional dress is expected. Many pilgrims wear traditional attire for darshan; cover shoulders and legs, and remove footwear before entering the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is often restricted inside the sanctum and around the deities. Follow posted notices and the instructions of temple staff, and ask permission before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Draksharama lies in the Godavari delta between Kakinada and Rajahmundry (Rajamahendravaram). Rajahmundry is the nearest major railhead and airport; from there and from Kakinada, buses and taxis reach the town, which is well connected by road.
